Prologo.2.full: **Dr Ferenc Halász – Society for Psychical Research, Budapest – *3 March 1923.***

Prologo.4.full: I write to you from the village I told you of, where I arrived on the evening train with an umbrella that proved entirely useless. The parish priest, a kind and very tired man, handed me the keys to the old sacristy. Behind a walnut wardrobe was a door, crudely bricked up; behind the door, six crates of documents.
Prologo.4.easy: I am writing to you from the village I told you about. I arrived on the evening train, with an umbrella that did not help at all. The parish priest, a kind and very tired man, gave me the keys to the old sacristy. Behind a wooden wardrobe there was a door closed up with bricks. Behind the door there were six crates full of documents.
Prologo.4.short: I write from the village I told you of. The priest gave me the keys to the old sacristy: behind a bricked-up door were six crates of documents.

Prologo.5.full: Séance minutes, letters never sent, torn diary pages, cuttings from the local gazette, telegrams whose ink has long since faded to violet. They cover fifty years and three generations of a single family: scientists, or something they liked to call by that name, who for half a century tried to speak with the dead. And not, it would seem, always without an answer.
Prologo.5.easy: There are séance records, letters that were never sent, torn diary pages, articles from the local newspaper and old telegrams. They tell the story of fifty years and three generations of the same family: scientists, or so they called themselves, who for half a century tried to talk to the dead. And it seems that sometimes someone answered.
Prologo.5.short: Minutes, letters, diaries and telegrams: fifty years of a family of scientists who tried to speak with the dead. And sometimes, it seems, were answered.

Prologo.6.full: I have resolved to sort and transcribe them before forming any judgement. The first document is the record of a wake. I ask you to read it as I did: with the scepticism the Society demands, and with the window shut.
Prologo.6.easy: I decided to put the documents in order and copy them before I judge anything. The first document is about a wake. I ask you to read it the way I did: with the doubt the Society asks for, and with the window closed.
Prologo.6.short: I have sorted and copied them. The first is the record of a wake: read it with scepticism, and with the window shut.

TkCreepy.2.full: For some days now, when you walk through {0}, people cross themselves. Children stop playing, dogs lower their tails. At night, under your window, there are bare footprints that lead up to the wall and never come back. Whatever it is, it has decided that you are the most interesting person in town.
TkCreepy.2.easy: For some days now, when you walk through {0}, people make the sign of the cross. Children stop playing and dogs lower their tails. At night, under your window, there are bare footprints: they go up to the wall and do not come back. Something has decided that you are the most interesting person in town.
TkCreepy.2.short: In {0} people cross themselves as you pass. Under your window, bare footprints lead to the wall and never come back. Something has chosen you.

TkCreepy.3.full: One morning, on the doorstep, you find a gift. Better not to wonder where it came from.
TkCreepy.3.easy: One morning you find a gift in front of your door. It is better not to ask where it comes from.

TkInsanity.2.full: At first it is only a murmur, like a room full of people in the house next door. Then you make out the words. Then the voices: an old woman looking for a ring, a child who counts to a hundred and starts again, a man who keeps repeating the same address. None of them seems to know they are dead.
TkInsanity.2.easy: At first you hear only a murmur, like many people in a room of the house next door. Then you understand the words. Then you hear the voices: an old woman looking for a ring, a child who counts to a hundred and starts again, a man who always repeats the same address. None of them seems to know they are dead.
TkInsanity.2.short: First a murmur, then voices: an old woman seeking a ring, a child counting, a man repeating an address. None of them knows they are dead.

TkInsanity.3.full: You take notes. You could not say whether you do it for science or to make them be quiet.

TkInsanity.4.full: Gain 1 Occult Knowledge. Return the {icon:StorybookToken} token to the supply.

TkOccult.2.full: One morning you open the Journal and find a page you did not write. The handwriting slants backwards, the ink is still wet, and the formula it describes is wrong in one place only, as if whoever wrote it wanted to see whether you would notice.
TkOccult.2.easy: One morning you open the Journal and find a page you did not write. The handwriting leans backwards and the ink is still wet. The formula on the page has only one mistake, as if the writer wanted to see if you would notice.
TkOccult.2.short: In the Journal is a page you did not write, the ink still wet, with a single mistake, like a test.

TkOccult.3.full: You notice. Beneath the correction, someone has added a single word: *"Good."*
TkOccult.3.easy: You notice. Under your correction, someone has written one word: *"Good."*

TkVP.2.full: Your name is going round {0}: at the market, in church, in the taverns. Some say it with fear, others with admiration, all of them in a low voice. A few days later a black-edged card invites you "to a dinner among people who will not resign themselves"; inside the envelope, as a courtesy, there is money.
TkVP.2.easy: In {0} everyone talks about you: at the market, in church, in the taverns. Some are afraid, others admire you, but they all speak quietly. A few days later you receive a card with a black border: it invites you "to a dinner among people who will not resign themselves". Inside the envelope, as a kindness, there is money.
TkVP.2.short: All {0} is talking about you, quietly. A black-edged card invites you "to a dinner among people who will not resign themselves", with money inside.

TkVP.3.full: The wax seal is black, with an open eye.

TkVP.4.full: Gain $2. Return the {icon:StorybookToken} token to the supply.

G1Intro.3.full: Father was buried on the Day of the Dead, under a thin rain that could not make up its mind to fall. The village came to the cemetery in good numbers, but stayed on the far side of the low wall: no one would go near the grave, and the gravedigger worked quickly, without looking in. It was said the old man had spent his last years shut up in the estate with machines that hummed through the night, and that from the windows of his laboratory there sometimes came a light of a colour no one could name.
G1Intro.3.easy: Father was buried on the Day of the Dead, under a light rain. Many people from the village came to the cemetery, but they stayed behind the low wall: no one wanted to go near the grave, and the gravedigger worked fast without looking in. People said that in his last years the old man had stayed shut up in the estate, with machines that made noise at night. Sometimes, from the windows of his laboratory, came a light of a strange colour that no one could describe.
G1Intro.3.short: Father was buried on the Day of the Dead. The village kept behind the cemetery wall: people said the old man had worked at night on humming machines, amid lights of a nameless colour.

G1Intro.4.full: The heirs had arrived on the coach the evening before, each from a different city, each with a trunk and the same letter from the notary. The estate was theirs, and with it the debts, the instruments, the animals in their cages and Father's Journal: a leather-bound notebook swollen with notes, sketches and formulae. On the last page he had written there was a single sentence, underlined twice, so hard that the pen had cut the paper:
G1Intro.4.easy: The heirs had arrived the evening before by coach. Each came from a different city, with a trunk and the same letter from the notary. Now the estate was theirs, and so were the debts, the instruments, the animals in the cages and Father's Journal: a leather notebook full of notes, drawings and formulae. On the last page there was only one sentence, underlined twice, so hard that the pen had cut the paper:
G1Intro.4.short: The heirs inherited the estate, the debts, the laboratory and Father's Journal. On its last page, one sentence, underlined so hard it cut the paper:

G1Intro.5.full: *"Death is not a closed door: it is a veil. And veils can be lifted."*

G1Intro.6.full: Father Anzelm blessed the body, closed his prayer book and told the heirs, loudly enough for everyone to hear, that he would pray for their souls with particular devotion.
G1Intro.6.easy: Father Anzelm blessed the body and closed his prayer book. Then he told the heirs, loudly enough for everyone to hear, that he would pray very hard for their souls.
G1Intro.6.short: Father Anzelm blessed the body and promised, loudly, to pray hard for the heirs' souls.

G1Intro.7.full: That night, in the estate, something began to knock on the walls.

G1ColpiA.4.full: I cannot sleep. The room they gave me was our father's: the bed still holds the shape of his body, and the air smells of camphor and acid. I put out the candle an hour ago when I hear the first knock.
G1ColpiA.4.easy: I cannot sleep. They gave me our father's room: the bed still has the shape of his body and the air smells of camphor and acid. I put out the candle an hour ago, and then I hear the first knock.
G1ColpiA.4.short: I lie awake in our father's room. Then I hear the first knock.

G1ColpiA.5.full: It comes from the wall behind the headboard. A sharp knock, like a knuckle on wood. Then two. Then one. Then nothing, for so long that I almost convince myself I dreamt it; and then they begin again, always the same, patient, like someone knocking at a door who knows there is someone at home.
G1ColpiA.5.easy: The sound comes from the wall behind the bed. A sharp knock, like a knuckle on wood. Then two knocks. Then one. Then nothing, for so long that I almost think I dreamt it. Then they start again, always the same and patient, like someone knocking at a door who knows someone is home.
G1ColpiA.5.short: Knocks on the wall behind the bed: one, two, one. Then silence, and again, patient, like someone who knows you are home.

G1ColpiA.6.full: In his library I saw a little French book on talking tables: one knock for yes, two for no. It comes back to me now, in the dark, and I wish it had not.
G1ColpiA.6.easy: In his library I saw a little French book about talking tables: one knock means yes, two mean no. I remember it now, in the dark, and I wish I did not.
G1ColpiA.6.short: I remember a little book from his library: one knock for yes, two for no. I wish I did not.

G1ColpiA.10.full: Pull the pillow over your head.

G1ColpiA.11.full: I sit up in bed and knock once, just once, with my knuckle, on the cold wall.

G1ColpiA.13.full: I ask, in the lowest voice, whether it is him. One knock. I ask whether he is at peace. Two knocks, so hard that the jug trembles on the chest of drawers. Then silence, and a smell of wax, though there is no candle lit in the room. In the morning my fingers are numb and the Journal lies open on the pillow, at a page I do not remember ever reading.
G1ColpiA.13.easy: I ask, very quietly, if it is him. One knock. I ask if he is at peace. Two knocks, so strong that the jug shakes on the chest of drawers. Then silence, and a smell of wax, even though no candle is lit in the room. In the morning my fingers are numb and the Journal is open on the pillow, at a page I do not remember ever reading.
G1ColpiA.13.short: Is it him? One knock. Is he at peace? Two knocks, very hard. In the morning the Journal lies open on my pillow, at a page I never read.

G1ColpiA.15.full: I wake the servant and send him to the village with the lantern. Father Anzelm arrives an hour later, his stole over his nightshirt and holy water in an apothecary's bottle. He blesses the wall, the bed, the window and, to be thorough, me as well.
G1ColpiA.15.easy: I wake the servant and send him to the village with the lantern. Father Anzelm arrives an hour later, with his stole over his nightshirt and holy water in a chemist's bottle. He blesses the wall, the bed, the window and, to be safe, me too.
G1ColpiA.15.short: I send for Father Anzelm. He comes in his nightshirt and blesses the wall, the bed and, to be thorough, me.

G1ColpiA.16.full: The knocking stops at once. The priest, however, lingers on the threshold longer than he needs to, looking around: the cages, the alembics, the Journal open on the table. Before leaving he shakes my hand and leaves me a few coins "for the household, until everything is in order". It feels more like a down payment than charity.
G1ColpiA.16.easy: The knocking stops at once. But the priest stays at the door longer than he needs to and looks around: the cages, the glass instruments, the Journal open on the table. Before he leaves he shakes my hand and gives me a few coins "for the household, until everything is in order". It feels more like an advance than help.
G1ColpiA.16.short: The knocking stops. The priest looks around a long time, then leaves me a few coins "for the household". It feels like a down payment.

G1ColpiA.18.full: I slip under the covers and press the pillow over my ears, as we did as children during storms. The knocking goes on for a long time, muffled, and at some point it seems to move: from the wall to the floor, from the floor to the headboard, a hand's breadth from my ear. Then, at last, it stops.
G1ColpiA.18.easy: I get under the covers and press the pillow on my ears, as we did as children during storms. The knocking goes on for a long time, more softly. At some point it seems to move: from the wall to the floor, from the floor to the bed, very close to my ear. Then, at last, it ends.
G1ColpiA.18.short: Under the covers, pillow over my ears, I hear the knocking creep closer, right up to my ear. Then at last it stops.

G1ColpiA.19.full: At dawn I draw back the curtain. On the wall, at the height of my head, the plaster has worn away in a small, regular circle, as if rubbed by a knuckle that had knocked there for years.
G1ColpiA.19.easy: At dawn I open the curtain. On the wall, at the height of my head, the plaster is worn away in a small, regular circle, as if a knuckle had knocked there for years.
G1ColpiA.19.short: At dawn there is a small worn circle on the wall, as if a knuckle had knocked there for years.

G1ColpiFine.2.full: At breakfast no one mentions the knocking. The coffee is too strong, the bread is yesterday's and everyone has dark rings under their eyes. Someone makes a joke about the mice in the attic, and no one laughs.
G1ColpiFine.2.easy: At breakfast no one talks about the knocking. The coffee is too strong, the bread is old and everyone looks tired. Someone makes a joke about the mice in the attic, but no one laughs.
G1ColpiFine.2.short: At breakfast no one mentions the knocking, and no one laughs at the jokes about mice.

G1ColpiFine.3.full: From the dining-room window you can see the village: a few wooden houses huddled around the church, smoke from the chimneys, the market waking up. It is a poor, suspicious place. But Father has left his heirs an estate, a laboratory and a name that still makes people lower their voices; and a name, for those who know how to use it, is worth as much as capital.
G1ColpiFine.3.easy: From the dining-room window you can see the village: a few wooden houses near the church, smoke from the chimneys, the market opening. It is a poor place where people do not trust strangers. But Father has left his heirs an estate, a laboratory and a name that still makes people speak quietly. And a name, if you know how to use it, is worth a lot of money.
G1ColpiFine.3.short: The village is poor and suspicious. But Father left his heirs an estate, a laboratory and a name that still makes people lower their voices: capital, for those who know how to use it.

G1R1.4.full: A caravan has stopped at the edge of the village. They say a woman travels in it who talks with the dead, and that the dead answer her.
G1R1.4.easy: A caravan has stopped near the village. People say that a woman travels in it who talks to the dead, and that the dead answer her.
G1R1.4.short: The wagon of a woman who talks with the dead has come to the village.

G1Seduta.3.full: Madame Vámos's wagon is painted midnight blue and covered in flaking gold stars. It has tall wheels, velvet curtains and, on the door, an open hand with an eye in its palm. It has stood at the edge of the village for three weeks, and in three weeks half the widows of {0} have climbed into it at least once, behind the priest's back.
G1Seduta.3.easy: Madame Vámos's wagon is painted dark blue and covered in worn gold stars. It has tall wheels, velvet curtains and, on the door, a picture of an open hand with an eye in the palm. It has been near the village for three weeks, and in that time half the widows of {0} have gone inside at least once, without telling the priest.
G1Seduta.3.short: Madame Vámos's wagon, midnight blue with a hand and an eye on the door, has stood there three weeks. Half the widows of {0} have secretly been inside.

G1Seduta.4.full: This morning the medium came to the estate in person. She is a small woman of indeterminate age, wrapped in a black shawl; she speaks softly, with an accent I cannot place, and has very white, very cold hands. She said she had heard the knocking. Not that someone had told her about the knocking: that she had *heard* it, from the road, passing the gate on the night of the dead.
G1Seduta.4.easy: This morning the medium came to the estate. She is a small woman, and it is hard to tell how old she is. She wears a black shawl, speaks softly with a strange accent, and has very white, very cold hands. She said she had heard the knocking. No one had told her about it: she had *heard* it herself, from the road, passing the gate on the night of the dead.
G1Seduta.4.short: The medium, small and ageless, came to the estate. She says she *heard* the knocking from the road, on the night of the dead.

G1Seduta.5.full: "Your father has something to say," she told us. "And he does not speak gladly to those who will not listen." Then she invited all of us to a séance in her wagon, tomorrow at midnight. She asked for no money. That, more than anything else, worries me.
G1Seduta.5.easy: "Your father has something to say," she told us. "And he does not like to speak to people who will not listen." Then she invited all of us to a séance in her wagon, tomorrow at midnight. She did not ask for money. That worries me more than anything.
G1Seduta.5.short: "Your father has something to say." She invited us to a séance tomorrow at midnight, free of charge. That is what worries me.

G1SedutaVoto.2.full: Each player takes a Voting token and chooses in secret. When everyone has chosen, reveal your votes together.

G1SedutaVoto.3.full: YAY: you attend Madame Vámos's séance.

G1SedutaVoto.4.full: NAY: you stay at the estate.

G1SedutaRacconto.2.full: No one goes. Madame Vámos lights the candles, sits at the little table and waits until dawn before empty chairs. The baker's boy, who passes by at four, swears he heard her talking to someone, and heard someone answer.
G1SedutaRacconto.2.easy: No one goes. Madame Vámos lights the candles, sits at the little table and waits until dawn in front of empty chairs. The baker's boy walks past at four and swears he heard her talking to someone, and heard someone answer.
G1SedutaRacconto.2.short: No one goes. Madame waits until dawn before empty chairs; the baker's boy swears he heard her talking, and someone answering.

G1SedutaRacconto.3.full: That night, at the estate, the knocking doubles. It knocks on every wall, every door, the headboard of every bed. It knocks like someone who has been left out in the cold.
G1SedutaRacconto.3.easy: That night, at the estate, there are twice as many knocks. They knock on every wall, every door, everyone's bed. They knock like someone who has been left outside in the cold.
G1SedutaRacconto.3.short: That night the knocking doubles, everywhere, like someone left out in the cold.

G1SedutaRacconto.4.full: All the heirs sit around the little round table, in the wagon that smells of incense and horse. Madame asks them to join hands; her fingers are icy. She recites something in a language no one recognises, then falls silent, and in the silence the table creaks, tilts and rises a hand's breadth off the floor, with every hand still upon it.
G1SedutaRacconto.4.easy: All the heirs sit around the little round table, in the wagon that smells of incense and horse. Madame asks them to hold hands; her fingers are freezing. She says something in a language no one knows, then she is silent. In the silence the table creaks, tips and rises a hand's width off the floor, with all their hands on it.
G1SedutaRacconto.4.short: The heirs join hands around the table. Madame recites unknown words, and the table rises a hand's breadth off the floor.

G1SedutaRacconto.5.full: It stays suspended for the space of a breath. Then it drops with a single, sharp knock. Madame opens her eyes and smiles like someone who has just had good news. "He recognised you," she says. "All of you."
G1SedutaRacconto.5.easy: It stays in the air for the time of one breath. Then it falls with a single sharp knock. Madame opens her eyes and smiles, like someone who has just had good news. "He recognised you," she says. "All of you."
G1SedutaRacconto.5.short: The table drops with one knock. Madame smiles: "He recognised you. All of you."

G1SedutaRacconto.6.full: Only some of the heirs climb into the wagon. The others stay at the estate, in front of the fire, telling one another that someone in the family must keep a little common sense.
G1SedutaRacconto.6.easy: Only some of the heirs get into the wagon. The others stay at the estate, in front of the fire, and tell each other that someone in the family must have a little common sense.
G1SedutaRacconto.6.short: Only some of the heirs go; the others stay home, out of common sense.

G1SedutaRacconto.7.full: Around one in the morning, from the direction of the village, comes a scream. Then another. Then a laugh, which could be anyone's. Those who return at dawn will not say what they saw; but their hands are as cold as Madame's, and all morning they keep looking at the walls.
G1SedutaRacconto.7.easy: Around one in the morning, a scream comes from the village. Then another. Then a laugh, but it is not clear whose. Those who come back at dawn do not want to say what they saw. But their hands are as cold as Madame's, and all morning they look at the walls.
G1SedutaRacconto.7.short: In the night, screams and a laugh from the village. Those who return at dawn say nothing, their hands cold as Madame's, eyes on the walls.

G1SedutaRacconto.8.full: Those who voted YAY gain 1 Occult Knowledge and 1 {icon:Insanity_Icon}.

G1SedutaRacconto.9.full: Those who voted NAY move back 1 space on the {icon:Creepy_Icon} track.

G1Patroni.3.full: **THE WITCH OF THE WAGON.** Last Sunday the Reverend Father Anzelm devoted his entire sermon to what he called, without mincing words, "the witch of the wagon". He reminded the faithful that the dead rest in the hands of God and not in the drawers of a little table, and that whoever disturbs them for money disturbs Him too. He then added, looking towards the pews at the back, that certain recently arrived families would do well to remember it.
G1Patroni.3.easy: **THE WITCH OF THE WAGON.** Last Sunday Father Anzelm spoke for the whole sermon about what he called, very clearly, "the witch of the wagon". He reminded the faithful that the dead rest with God, not inside a little table, and that whoever disturbs them for money also disturbs God. Then, looking at the pews at the back, he said that some families who had arrived recently should remember this.
G1Patroni.3.short: **THE WITCH OF THE WAGON.** Father Anzelm's sermon was about "the witch of the wagon": the dead rest with God, and certain newly arrived families would do well to remember it.

G1Patroni.4.full: The sermon was much appreciated. On Monday, however, this newspaper observed an unusual coming and going of ladies in black on the road to the estate. The widows of {0} have lost husbands, sons and brothers to the cold, the fevers and hunger; they want news of their loved ones, and for one's loved ones, as everyone knows, no expense is spared.
G1Patroni.4.easy: People liked the sermon very much. On Monday, however, this newspaper saw many ladies dressed in black coming and going on the road to the estate. The widows of {0} have lost husbands, sons and brothers to the cold, fevers and hunger. They want news of their loved ones, and for loved ones, as everyone knows, people pay gladly.
G1Patroni.4.short: On Monday, though, many widows of {0} take the road to the estate: they want news of their dead, and will pay for it.

G1R2.6.full: Someone in the village writes letters, and does not sign them. The envelopes arrive without stamps, and no one has seen them arrive.
G1R2.6.easy: Someone in the village writes letters without signing them. The envelopes come without stamps, and no one sees them arrive.

G1Lettere.2.full: In the middle years the family begins to receive post the postman never delivered. The letters appear under the door, in the bread basket, once even inside Father's Journal, locked in the writing desk. They are envelopes of heavy paper, with no address and no signature, sealed with black wax; in the wax, an open eye.
G1Lettere.2.easy: In the middle years the family receives letters that the postman never brought. The letters appear under the door, in the bread basket, once even inside Father's Journal, locked in the desk. They are envelopes of heavy paper, with no address and no signature, closed with black wax. In the wax there is the picture of an open eye.
G1Lettere.2.short: Letters arrive that no one delivered, even inside the locked Journal. No address, no signature: only an open eye in black wax.

G1Lettere.3.full: Inside, each time, a few lines in an elegant, old-fashioned hand. The **Circle of the Last Hour** greets the heirs of the great scientist, knows their work, admires their courage and wishes to meet them, one by one, somewhere discreet. They need only present themselves at the address given and speak the right word.
G1Lettere.3.easy: Inside there are always a few lines, in elegant, old-fashioned handwriting. G2Telegrafo.3.easy: In the second volume of the Journal, between a recipe for preserving tissue and a blacksmith's bill, I found the design. There are three drawings in ink, made with a care Grandfather gave to nothing else. He calls it the **Telegraph of the Dead**.
G2Telegrafo.3.short: In the Journal I found Grandfather's design, drawn with rare care: the **Telegraph of the Dead**.

G2Telegrafo.4.full: A battery of glass jars; miles of copper wire wound around a soft-iron core; a keyboard of twenty-six bone keys; and at its centre a needle suspended in a flask full of a gas he calls "veil air". A very sensitive needle is enough to read them.
G2Telegrafo.4.short: Glass jars, copper wire, a bone keyboard and a needle in a flask of "veil air". The dead, he believed, barely move the current: a sensitive needle can read them.

G2Nebbia.3.full: **THE FOG WILL NOT LIFT.** For eleven days a dense, whitish fog has covered {0} from dawn to dusk, and from dusk to dawn. The district doctor speaks of miasmas from the pond; the apothecary, of fumes from the estate; Father Anzelm, of a punishment. Lanterns light no further than three paces. Yesterday the coach arrived six hours late: the coachman swears he drove in circles around the cemetery all night.
G2Nebbia.3.easy: **THE FOG WILL NOT LIFT.** For eleven days a thick white fog has covered {0} day and night. The doctor says it comes from the pond, the chemist says it comes from the estate, Father Anzelm says it is a punishment. Lanterns light only three steps ahead. Yesterday the coach arrived six hours late: the driver swears he went round and round the cemetery all night.
G2Nebbia.3.short: **THE FOG WILL NOT LIFT.** For eleven days fog has covered {0} day and night. The coach circled the cemetery all night.

G2Nebbia.4.full: Stranger still are the accounts this newspaper continues to receive. Mrs Tóth saw her husband, nine years dead, waiting for her at the corner by the apothecary. The baker heard his mother calling him from the oven. Three children played all afternoon with a friend none of the adults saw, and whose name no one knows. Readers are advised not to go out unless necessary, and not to answer anyone who calls their name from the fog.
G2Nebbia.4.easy: Even stranger are the stories that reach the newspaper. Mrs Tóth saw her husband, dead for nine years, waiting for her at the corner by the chemist's. The baker heard his mother calling him from the oven. Three children played all afternoon with a friend no adult saw, and whose name no one knows. We advise readers not to go out unless they must, and not to answer anyone who calls their name from the fog.
G2Nebbia.4.short: The dead are seen in the fog: a husband nine years buried, a mother calling from the oven, a nameless child. Do not answer anyone who calls you from the fog.

G2Asilo.2.short: At the Asylum Program, Father Anzelm treats the fog's "possessed": people who speak in others' voices and knock on the walls for hours.

G2Asilo.3.full: The cure is harsh: icy baths, prayers, leather straps, silence. In some way it does you good to see how thin the line is between them and you. But the man in cell number seven, when you pass, stops knocking and greets you by your name, in your grandfather's voice.

G3Intro.4.full: The telegram reached the new heirs in distant cities, in offices, laboratories and colleges. When they stepped off the train (for now the train went there too) they found a small town that no longer resembled the village of the family stories: street lamps along the main road, a telegraph office, a bank with columns of imitation marble and, in the café on the square, a phonograph that played Viennese waltzes for anyone who dropped in a coin.

When they got off the train (now the train went there too) they found a small town very different from the village of the family stories. G3Intro.4.short: The telegram reached the new heirs far away. Off the train, they found a modern little town: street lamps, a telegraph, a bank and a phonograph playing waltzes.

G3Citta.2.full: And there was the Circle. The Circle of the Last Hour no longer needed to hide, nor to advertise: it owned the undertaker's, half the buildings on the square and the majority of the town council. Its members wore a small silver eye in their buttonholes, and wore it with pride.

G3Citta.2.short: The Circle now owned the undertaker's, half the square and the town council. Its members proudly wore a silver eye.

G3Citta.3.full: And there was the Church. After years of sermons, trials and excommunications, the bishop had got what he wanted: the Circle of the Last Hour was outlawed, its séances a crime, and whoever spoke with the dead ended up before the church court. Father Benedek, Father Anzelm's successor, kept a register of names; the family's appeared in it more than once.
G3Citta.3.easy: And there was the Church. G3Citta.3.short: The Church had won: the Circle was outlawed and séances a crime. Father Benedek kept a register of names, and the family's appeared more than once.

G3Telegrafo.2.short: At the last wire the Telegraph switches itself on, and a hum fills the estate, perhaps the town.

Membership of the Circle of the Last Hour collapses within a week; on the square someone throws stones at its windows.
G3Conteggio.3.easy: **THE SCANDAL OF THE CIRCLE.** The Gazette publishes on its front page, across six columns, the evidence found by Dr Lukács: the blacksmith's receipts, the exposed shops, the confessions of two former members. In a week almost everyone leaves the Circle of the Last Hour, and on the square someone throws stones at its windows.
G3Conteggio.3.short: **THE SCANDAL OF THE CIRCLE.** The Gazette prints Lukács's evidence. Within a week the Circle loses its members, and stones fly on the square.

G3Conteggio.4.full: Madame Vámos, summoned by the magistrate, does not appear. They say she has packed her bags; they also say she has no bags to pack.
G3Conteggio.4.easy: Madame Vámos is called by the judge, but she does not come. Some say she has packed her bags. Others say she has no bags to pack.

G3Conteggio.5.full: At the estate, that night, the knocking on the walls is fainter than usual. Almost shy.
G3Conteggio.5.easy: That night, at the estate, the knocking on the walls is softer than usual. Almost shy.

G3Conteggio.7.full: No one has touched the fronts. The Circle's shops stay open late, with spotless windows and few customers; Dr Lukács writes furious letters to the Gazette, which does not publish them.
G3Conteggio.7.easy: No one has touched the fake shops. The Circle's shops stay open late, with perfect windows and few customers. Dr Lukács writes angry letters to the Gazette, but the Gazette does not print them.
G3Conteggio.7.short: No one has touched the fronts, and the Gazette does not print Lukács's furious letters.

G3Conteggio.8.full: The Circle, in silence, gives thanks: one morning each heir finds a fresh black carnation on the doorstep.
G3Conteggio.8.easy: The Circle, without a word, says thank you: one morning each heir finds a fresh black carnation in front of the door.

G3Conteggio.9.full: One front has fallen, and what was behind it went round the town in a day. But the others are still standing, and the Circle denies everything with great dignity.
G3Conteggio.9.easy: One fake shop has been exposed, and in a day the whole town knows what it was hiding. But the others are still open, and the Circle denies everything with great dignity.
G3Conteggio.9.short: One front has fallen, but the others hold, and the Circle denies everything.

G3GrandeSeduta.3.full: On the last night of 1905 {0} gathers in the great hall of the town hall: the mayor, the council, the Circle, the parish, Dr Lukács with his notebook and, in the middle, the family of the estate. Two hundred people seated in concentric circles, hands joined with their neighbours', the lamps out. No one remembers who called the meeting. Everyone, however, has come.
G3GrandeSeduta.3.easy: On the last night of 1905 all of {0} meets in the great hall of the town hall: the mayor, the council, the Circle, the parish, Dr Lukács with his notebook and, in the middle, the family of the estate. Two hundred people sit in circles, each holding their neighbours' hands, and the lights are off. No one remembers who called them. But everyone has come.
G3GrandeSeduta.3.short: On the last night of 1905 two hundred people sit in circles in the town hall of {0}, hand in hand, in the dark. No one knows who summoned them, but all have come.

G3GrandeSeduta.4.full: At a quarter to midnight the knocking begins. Not on the walls: everywhere. In the floor, in the ceiling, in the chairs, in each person's chest. Fifty-seven years after that first night, the veil has never been so thin.
G3GrandeSeduta.4.easy: At a quarter to twelve the knocking begins. Not on the walls: everywhere. In the floor, in the ceiling, in the chairs, in everyone's chest. Fifty-seven years after that first night, the veil has never been so thin.
G3GrandeSeduta.4.short: At a quarter to midnight the knocking starts everywhere, even in their chests. The veil has never been so thin.

G3GrandeSeduta.5.easy: Someone has brought the Telegraph from the estate on a cart and connected it to the town hall's electric wires. The needle taps by itself, impatient, waiting for instructions.
G3GrandeSeduta.5.short: The Telegraph, wired to the town hall's lights, taps by itself, impatient.

FinaleSquarciato.3.full: Dear Doctor, you ask me what happened on the night of 31 December 1905. I will tell you, even though you will not believe me, and even though you need only step out of the sacristy and take a few steps across the square to see it with your own eyes.
FinaleSquarciato.3.easy: Dear Doctor, you ask me what happened on the night of 31 December 1905. I will tell you, even if you will not believe me. And even though you only need to leave the sacristy and walk a little on the square to see it with your own eyes.
FinaleSquarciato.3.short: Dear Doctor, you ask about the night of 31 December 1905. You will not believe me, but you need only step into the square to see.

FinaleSquarciato.4.full: We voted to open. The Telegraph, or the medium, or our joined hands (I no longer know which was the key) turned in the lock, and the veil tore like an old curtain. There was no flash, no thunder. Only a great cold, and then the door of the hall opening by itself, and people coming in. People we knew. People we had buried.
FinaleSquarciato.4.easy: We voted to open. The Telegraph, or the medium, or our joined hands (I no longer know what the key was) turned in the lock, and the veil tore like an old curtain. There was no flash and no thunder. Only a great cold. Then the door of the hall opened by itself, and people came in. People we knew. People we had buried.
FinaleSquarciato.4.short: We voted to open, and the veil tore like an old curtain. In a great cold, people we had buried came in through the door.

FinaleSquarciato.5.full: They stayed. In {0} the dead walk with the living, sit at their tables, vote in the council, complain about the price of bread. At first you could tell them apart: they were paler, quieter, and cast no shadow. Now it is no longer so simple.
FinaleSquarciato.5.easy: They stayed. In {0} the dead walk with the living, eat at their tables, vote in the council, complain about the price of bread. At first it was easy to recognise them: they were paler, quieter, and had no shadow. Now it is not so easy.
FinaleSquarciato.5.short: They stayed. In {0} the dead live among the living. At first you could tell them apart. Not any more.

FinaleSquarciato.6.full: You ask me from which side of the veil I am writing to you. Honestly, Doctor, some years ago I stopped asking myself.
FinaleSquarciato.6.easy: You ask me which side of the veil I am writing from. Honestly, Doctor, I stopped asking myself some years ago.

FinaleSilenzio.3.full: Dear Doctor, the Telegraph was finished. One had only to turn a dial to hear Father's voice; one had only to turn it the other way to close the door for ever. We voted to close it.
FinaleSilenzio.3.easy: Dear Doctor, the Telegraph was finished. You only had to turn a dial to hear Father's voice, and turn it the other way to close the door for ever. We voted to close it.
FinaleSilenzio.3.short: Dear Doctor, with the Telegraph we could hear Father or close the door for ever. We voted to close it.

FinaleSilenzio.4.full: The machine screamed for an hour, then fell silent. Since that night no séance has ever worked again: not in {0}, not in Vienna, not in London. Tables stay on the floor, mediums have taken to the stage, and your Society studies nothing with great rigour. I apologise.
FinaleSilenzio.4.easy: The machine screamed for an hour, then stopped. Since that night no séance has ever worked again: not in {0}, not in Vienna, not in London. Tables stay on the floor, mediums work in the theatre, and your Society studies nothing very seriously. I am sorry.
FinaleSilenzio.4.short: The machine screamed, then fell silent. Since then no séance has worked anywhere. My apologies to your Society.

FinaleSilenzio.5.full: Father's voice, too, stayed on the other side. We will never know what he wanted to tell us. Sometimes, at night, I lay my hand on the wall of my room, the one where they used to knock, and wait. The wall is cold, and mute, and I sleep very well.
FinaleSilenzio.5.easy: Father's voice also stayed on the other side. We will never know what he wanted to tell us. Sometimes, at night, I put my hand on the wall of my room, the one where they used to knock, and wait. The wall is cold and silent, and I sleep very well.
FinaleSilenzio.5.short: We will never know what Father wanted to tell us. Sometimes at night I touch the wall where they used to knock. It is silent, and I sleep very well.

FinaleSilenzio.6.full: That is what I cannot forgive myself.

FinaleTruffa.3.full: Dear Doctor, it was all a trick. Dr Lukács had always said so, and in the end we proved it in front of all {0}: threads of black silk to lift the table, a smith in on it for the knocking in the walls, gauze and phosphorus for the ectoplasm, and a network of informers (widows, innkeepers, the sexton) who told the Circle everyone's secrets. The voices of the dead were the voices of the living, well paid.
FinaleTruffa.3.easy: Dear Doctor, it was all a trick. Dr Lukács had always said so, and in the end we proved it in front of all {0}. There were black silk threads to lift the table, a blacksmith working with them for the knocking in the walls, gauze and phosphorus for the ectoplasm, and many spies (widows, innkeepers, the sexton) who told the Circle everyone's secrets. The voices of the dead were the voices of the living, well paid.
FinaleTruffa.3.short: Dear Doctor, it was all a trick: silk threads, a smith in on it, gauze and phosphorus, a network of informers. The voices of the dead were the living, well paid.

FinaleTruffa.4.full: Our family became famous. We wrote books, gave lectures in Budapest and Paris, exposed thirty-two mediums in eleven countries. Your Society even awarded us a medal, which I keep in a drawer.
FinaleTruffa.4.easy: Our family became famous. We wrote books, gave talks in Budapest and Paris and exposed thirty-two cheating mediums in eleven countries. Your Society even gave us a medal, which I keep in a drawer.
FinaleTruffa.4.short: We became famous: books, lectures, thirty-two mediums exposed. And a medal, in a drawer.

FinaleTruffa.5.full: I am writing, though, to tell you something I have never said in public. The smith, when questioned, confessed to having knocked on the walls of the estate for twenty years, on the Circle's orders. But the knocking on the first night, on 2 November 1848, was not his doing: he was six years old at the time.
FinaleTruffa.5.easy: But I am writing to tell you something I have never said in public. The blacksmith, when questioned, admitted he had knocked on the walls of the estate for twenty years, because the Circle asked him to. But the knocking on the first night, 2 November 1848, was not his: he was six years old then.
FinaleTruffa.5.short: But the smith, who knocked for the Circle for twenty years, was six years old on the first night, in 1848.

FinaleTruffa.6.full: And on certain nights, even today, someone knocks at the estate. One knock, then two, then one.
FinaleTruffa.6.easy: And some nights, even today, someone knocks at the estate. One knock, then two, then one.

FinaleVoce.3.full: Dear Doctor, the Telegraph tapped for three days and three nights. The needle ran over the bone keys faster than we could transcribe, and we took turns at the table, in two-hour shifts, our fingers black with ink. It was him, beyond any doubt: the same abbreviations, the same spelling mistakes, the same impatience as in the Journal.
FinaleVoce.3.easy: Dear Doctor, the Telegraph tapped for three days and three nights. The needle ran over the bone keys faster than we could write, and we took turns at the table every two hours, with fingers black with ink. It was him, without doubt: the same abbreviations, the same mistakes, the same impatience as in the Journal.
FinaleVoce.3.short: Dear Doctor, the Telegraph tapped for three days and nights, and we transcribed in shifts. It was him: the same mistakes, the same impatience as the Journal.

FinaleVoce.4.full: He did not ask how we were. He did not tell us what it was like on the other side. He dictated, and nothing else: formulae, tables, drawings described point by point. It was the last part of his Masterwork, the part death had kept him from finishing. At the end of the third night the needle stopped, went back to the centre and tapped out one last sentence: *"Now leave me in peace."*
FinaleVoce.4.easy: He did not ask how we were. He did not tell us what it was like on the other side. He just dictated: formulae, tables, drawings explained point by point. It was the last part of his Masterwork, the part death had not let him finish. At the end of the third night the needle stopped, went back to the middle and wrote one last sentence: *"Now leave me in peace."*
FinaleVoce.4.short: He asked nothing: he dictated the last part of his Masterwork. Then the needle tapped: *"Now leave me in peace."*

FinaleVoce.5.full: We did. The Masterwork is finished, Doctor, and was published under his name. The Telegraph is dismantled, in the attic. We have never switched it on again.
FinaleVoce.5.easy: We did. The Masterwork is finished, Doctor, and it was published with his name. The Telegraph is taken apart, in the attic. We have never switched it on again.
FinaleVoce.5.short: The Masterwork was published. The Telegraph is in the attic, dismantled.

FinaleVoce.6.full: Not out of respect: for fear that someone else might answer.

FinaleRogo.3.full: Dear Doctor, the Church won, and it was not a gentle victory. The bishop came to {0} in the spring of 1906 with a decree, two gendarmes and a list of names. Our family was at the top.
FinaleRogo.3.easy: Dear Doctor, the Church won, and it was not a gentle victory. The bishop came to {0} in the spring of 1906 with a decree, two policemen and a list of names. Our family's name was first.
FinaleRogo.3.short: Dear Doctor, the Church won. The bishop came in 1906 with a list of names, and ours was first.

FinaleRogo.4.full: The Circle's premises burned on the night of Pentecost. The fire, somehow, leapt the road and reached the estate. The greenhouses burned, the cages, the laboratory, the volumes of the Journal. The Telegraph, as it melted, made a sound the firemen described as a wail.
FinaleRogo.4.easy: The Circle's building burned on the night of Pentecost. Somehow the fire crossed the road and reached the estate. The greenhouses, the cages, the laboratory and the volumes of the Journal burned. The Telegraph, as it melted, made a noise the firemen described as a cry of pain.
FinaleRogo.4.short: At Pentecost the Circle burned, and the fire reached the estate. The Telegraph melted with a wail.

FinaleRogo.5.full: On the ashes the bishop had a chapel built, dedicated to the souls in purgatory. I go there every Sunday, like everyone. The priest says its walls are the quietest in the diocese, and he is right: no one ever knocks there.
FinaleRogo.5.easy: On the ashes the bishop had a chapel built for the souls in purgatory. I go there every Sunday, like everyone. The priest says its walls are the quietest in the diocese, and he is right: no one ever knocks there.
FinaleRogo.5.short: A chapel now stands on the ashes. Its walls are the quietest in the diocese.

FinaleRogo.6.full: But in the crypt, beneath the altar, where the laboratory used to be, the sexton stopped going down years ago.
FinaleRogo.6.easy: But in the crypt, under the altar, where the laboratory used to be, the sexton has not gone down for years.

FinaleSocieta.3.full: Dear Doctor, you ask me who governs {0}. Formally the town council, and a mayor who still bears the Bódi name. In practice, since that night in 1905, every decision passes first across a little table.
FinaleSocieta.3.easy: Dear Doctor, you ask me who is in charge in {0}. On paper, the town council, and a mayor who is still called Bódi. In reality, since that night in 1905, every decision goes first across a little table.
FinaleSocieta.3.short: Dear Doctor, the council governs {0}. But since 1905 every decision passes first across a little table.

FinaleSocieta.4.full: The Great Séance ended with our family at the head of the Circle of the Last Hour, and the Circle welcomed us as one welcomes a long-awaited heir. The undertaker's, the bank, the newspaper, the school: everything belongs to us, or to someone who owes us a favour. The widows bless us. So, they say, do the dead.
FinaleSocieta.4.easy: The Great Séance ended with our family leading the Circle of the Last Hour, and the Circle welcomed us like an heir it had waited for a long time. The undertaker's, the bank, the newspaper, the school: everything is ours, or belongs to someone who owes us a favour. The widows bless us. And, people say, so do the dead.
FinaleSocieta.4.short: We lead the Circle, and everything is ours or owes us a favour. The widows bless us, and so do the dead.

FinaleSocieta.5.full: Do not imagine it is a comfortable power. Every Thursday evening we consult those who came before us, and the dead are demanding counsellors: they forget nothing, forgive nothing, and have all the time in the world.
FinaleSocieta.5.easy: Do not think it is a comfortable power. Every Thursday evening we ask advice from those who came before us, and the dead are difficult advisers: they forget nothing, forgive nothing, and have all the time in the world.
FinaleSocieta.5.short: But the dead are demanding counsellors: they forget nothing, forgive nothing, and have all the time in the world.

FinaleSocieta.6.full: I write to you with their permission. They asked me to tell you that your work has been noticed, and that, whenever you wish, there will be a chair for you too at our table. I advise you not to wish it.
FinaleSocieta.6.easy: I am writing with their permission. They asked me to tell you that your work has been noticed, and that, whenever you want, there will be a chair for you too at our table. I advise you not to want it.
FinaleSocieta.6.short: They ask me to tell you there is a chair for you at our table. I advise you not to want it.

FinalePossessione.3.full: Dear Doctor, I recognise you by your handwriting. You, on the other hand, will not recognise mine: it is not that of the person who signs this letter. Since the night of the Great Séance, when the vial broke in the hands of {0}, this hand has written for me.
FinalePossessione.3.easy: Dear Doctor, I recognise you by your handwriting. You, however, will not recognise mine: it is not the handwriting of the person who signs this letter. Since the night of the Great Séance, when the vial broke in the hands of {0}, this hand has written for me.
FinalePossessione.3.short: Dear Doctor, you will not recognise my hand. Since the vial broke in the hands of {0}, this hand has written for me.

FinalePossessione.4.full: Allow me to introduce myself, though perhaps you have already understood: Eszter Vámos, consoler. For half a century they called me a fraud, a witch, a prophetess, a saint. They were all a little right. The secret of eternal life, Doctor, was never for sale: it was in that vial. One had only to find the right person, mad enough to let me in.
FinalePossessione.4.easy: Let me introduce myself, though perhaps you have already understood: Eszter Vámos, consoler. For fifty years they called me a cheat, a witch, a prophet, a saint. They were all a little right. The secret of eternal life, Doctor, was not for sale: it was in that vial. I only had to find the right person, mad enough to let me in.
FinalePossessione.4.short: I am Eszter Vámos, consoler. The secret of eternal life was in that vial: I only needed someone mad enough to let me in.

FinalePossessione.5.full: This body is younger than mine, and has warmer hands: I use it with care. I write to you because you are reading my minutes, and I have always had a soft spot for those who read me attentively.
FinalePossessione.5.easy: This body is younger than mine and has warmer hands: I use it carefully. I am writing to you because you are reading my records, and I have always liked people who read me carefully.
FinalePossessione.5.short: This body is young, and I use it with care. I write because you read my minutes so attentively.

FinalePossessione.6.full: Come and see me, when you have finished. I will keep an empty chair for you.

FinaleNebbia.3.full: I searched for a long time for a living heir to question, as I did for the other documents in the file. I found none. The papers stop on the night of 31 December 1905, halfway through a record: the veil was torn, and the family voted not to cross it. Then, says the last line, "the fog came in through the windows".
FinaleNebbia.3.easy: I looked for a long time for a living heir to question, as I did for the other documents in the file. I did not find one. The papers end on the night of 31 December 1905, in the middle of a record: the veil was torn, and the family voted not to cross it. Then, says the last line, "the fog came in through the windows".
FinaleNebbia.3.short: I found no living heir. The papers stop on 31 December 1905: the veil was torn, the family did not cross it, and "the fog came in through the windows".

FinaleNebbia.4.full: Since 1906 {0} no longer appears on any map. Trains do not stop there, the telegraph does not answer, and travellers who try to reach it tell of walking for hours in a white fog, around a cemetery, before finding themselves back where they started.
FinaleNebbia.4.easy: Since 1906 {0} is no longer on any map. Trains do not stop there, the telegraph does not answer, and travellers who try to get there say they walked for hours in a white fog, around a cemetery, before finding themselves back where they started.
FinaleNebbia.4.short: Since 1906 {0} has vanished from the maps. Those who try to reach it walk for hours in the fog, around a cemetery, and end up where they began.

FinaleNebbia.5.full: You will ask me, then, where I found these crates. I ask myself too. I remember the evening train, the umbrella, the kind and very tired priest. I do not remember how I left the village.
FinaleNebbia.5.easy: So you will ask me where I found these crates. I ask myself too. I remember the evening train, the umbrella, the kind and very tired priest. I do not remember how I left the village.
FinaleNebbia.5.short: Where did I find these crates? I remember the train, the umbrella, the priest. I do not remember leaving the village.

FinaleNebbia.6.full: I am writing from my study in Budapest. From the window, for three days, I have seen nothing but fog. And someone, politely, is knocking.
FinaleNebbia.6.easy: I am writing from my study in Budapest. For three days I have seen only fog from the window. And someone, politely, is knocking.
